label: Co-teaching & Workplace Culture
blurb: Co-teaching and the everyday habits of a Taiwanese staffroom.
blurbZh: 協同教學，以及台灣辦公室的日常默契。

questions.stem: You propose a new activity to your co-teacher. She says: “We'll study it and see.” 我們再研究看看. What has she most likely told you?
options: No — expressed in a way that avoids putting you in the wrong
She is interested and will get back to you
She needs more information before deciding
She wants you to write a formal proposal
questions.why: Direct refusal puts the other person in the wrong, so it is often avoided. “We'll study it and see”, “that might be a little difficult”, “maybe next semester”, a pause and a change of subject, and enthusiastic agreement followed by nothing — all of these are usually no. Learning to hear it saves you from pushing.

questions.stem: You suspect the answer was no, but you genuinely need to know. What is the best way to ask?
options: Ask again in the next staff meeting so there is a clear record
Ask privately, and offer an easy exit: “Is this worth pursuing, or should I drop it? Either is fine.”
Ask a third colleague what she really meant
Proceed as if the answer was yes and see what happens
questions.why: Pushing in public forces someone to refuse you explicitly, which is the thing the indirect answer was designed to avoid — you get your answer and pay for it. Asking privately with an easy exit lets them be direct without cost, and most people will be.

questions.stem: In Taiwanese school culture, “face” (面子) is best understood as:
options: A person's standing in front of others — which is what lets them do their job
Emotional fragility
Personal vanity
A formal system of rank
questions.why: Standing is functional, not decorative: it is what allows a teacher to manage a class and a director to run a department. Damaging it does not merely embarrass someone, it makes their work harder — which is why the cost of a public correction is so much larger than it looks.

questions.stem: Your co-teacher gives students a piece of grammar information you know is wrong. What should you do?
options: Correct it immediately so students are not misled
Say nothing, and mention it privately afterwards
Ask the students what they think the answer is
Correct it gently, framing it as a regional difference
questions.why: A public correction in front of thirty students costs her the standing she needs to manage them, and they will remember the correction more than the grammar. Mention it afterwards and it can be fixed next lesson at no cost. One wrong item for one day is a smaller problem than a co-teacher who cannot rely on you.

questions.stem: You intend to raise a problem at Friday's staff meeting. What should you do first?
options: Circulate a written summary in advance
Prepare your points carefully and present them clearly
Tell the person concerned beforehand
Nothing — meetings are the correct place to raise problems
questions.why: Being blindsided in front of colleagues is the injury, usually more than the substance. Telling them first also frequently solves it before the meeting — and decisions here are often reached beforehand anyway, in conversations between the people concerned. That is where the work happens.

questions.stem: A staff meeting is conducted entirely in Chinese. The most considerate approach is:
options: Ask your co-teacher to translate as it goes
Ask for the meeting to be held in English
Ask for a two-minute summary afterwards
Skip such meetings, since you cannot follow them
questions.why: Live translation means your colleague cannot participate in her own meeting; a summary afterwards costs her two minutes. Attending even without understanding is also worth more than it seems — presence is read as commitment, and you will catch more over a term than you expect.

questions.stem: You are invited to a staff dinner at the end of a hard term, and you are exhausted. The best move is:
options: Decline politely; nobody will mind
Go, even if only for part of it
Decline but send a gift
Go only if your co-teacher goes
questions.why: Attendance is most of it, and leaving early is entirely normal. Turning up for an hour is read as being part of the group; a polite decline is read — usually wrongly, but consistently — as not wanting to be. This is the cheapest investment available to you all year.

questions.stem: A colleague invites you to their wedding. You have no idea what is expected. What should you do?
options: Bring a wrapped gift instead of money, to be safe
Attend but give nothing, since you are a foreign guest
Give a generous amount to be safe
Ask a colleague what amount is appropriate for the red envelope
questions.why: Asking is completely normal and nobody will think less of you for it — guessing is how people get it wrong in both directions. Amounts vary by relationship and region, and a colleague can tell you in one sentence. Attending matters more than the amount.

questions.stem: A parent gives you an expensive gift after their child's exam results improve. What should you do?
options: Accept graciously; refusing would cause loss of face
Accept and share it with the office
Decline politely and tell your school
Accept but give something of equal value in return
questions.why: Public-school staff are subject to rules on receiving gifts, and the timing here — after results — is exactly the pattern those rules exist for. Decline warmly, and tell your school so that the record shows you did. A red envelope is always declined. Small shared items like fruit for the office are a different matter.

questions.stem: A colleague asks your age, your salary, and whether you are married. This is usually:
options: An intrusion you should politely shut down
Preparation for a formal report
A test of whether you will fit in
Ordinary friendliness and an attempt to place you socially
questions.why: In many countries these questions are off-limits; here they are usually the small talk of getting to know someone. You are not obliged to answer any of them, and a light deflection with a question back works perfectly — but reading them as rudeness will make you lonely for no reason.

questions.stem: You have a genuine complaint about how your co-teacher runs the class. The best first step is:
options: Write a clear, polite email so there is a record
Message it on LINE so it can be discussed asynchronously
Raise it with the Director of Academic Affairs
Speak in person, privately, opening with the shared goal
questions.why: A written grievance is permanent, forwardable, and reads far colder than you meant it — and it is now a document rather than a conversation. In person, privately, opening with what you both want (“I want this class to go better for both of us”) and asking a question rather than making an accusation, is the version that can still end well.

questions.stem: Going over a colleague's head to their director is:
options: Normal escalation, expected when a problem persists
Expensive and rarely recoverable — reserve it for genuine necessity
Always inappropriate, whatever the issue
The fastest route to a solution
questions.why: It is the most expensive move available to you and the relationship usually does not recover. Escalate in order, and slowly. The clear exception is anything covered by Modules 4, 5 or 6 — where the duty runs regardless of hierarchy, and where saying plainly that you have no discretion is both true and protective of the relationship.

questions.stem: In the lead-and-support model, which pattern suggests something has gone wrong?
options: The foreign teacher always leading and never planning
The lead role alternating between the two teachers
The co-teacher circulating and managing behavior some lessons
Both teachers occasionally splitting the class
questions.why: Support roles should alternate. If you are permanently the entertainer at the front and never in the planning, you are a resource rather than a colleague — and it usually means the conversation about roles never happened, not that anyone decided it should be this way.

questions.stem: What single conversation is most likely to improve a co-teaching relationship?
options: An honest discussion about the students' weaknesses
A shared social activity outside school
Agreeing who plans, who leads, who handles behavior, and when you swap
A written agreement about responsibilities
questions.why: Most pairs never explicitly agree any of it: they improvise for a year, each quietly frustrated, each assuming the other prefers it this way. The conversation takes ten minutes and is worth having once per unit rather than once per year — and it is the one that changes what next year looks like.

questions.stem: “可能有點困難” — “that might be a little difficult” — usually means:
options: No
More resources are needed
The task is hard but achievable
A decision has been deferred
questions.why: It is one of the standard indirect refusals, alongside “we'll study it and see” and “maybe next semester”. Taken literally it sounds like an obstacle to solve; heard correctly it is an answer already given.

questions.stem: When should you tell a colleague that you plan to raise their issue in a meeting?
options: Immediately after the meeting
There is no need to tell them
Beforehand, always
Only if the issue is serious
questions.why: Always, and without exception. Being surprised in front of colleagues is the injury. Telling them first also often means the meeting is no longer necessary.

questions.stem: Which is the best gift to bring back from a trip home?
options: Something to share in the staff room
An individual gift for your favorite student
An expensive gift for the principal
Nothing; gifts are inappropriate
questions.why: Something shared for the office is always well received and creates no awkwardness for anyone. Individual gifts to students are a Module 5 problem, and an expensive gift to the principal creates precisely the situation the gift rules are written about.

questions.stem: You do not understand what was decided in a Chinese-language meeting. What should you do?
options: Ask a student to explain
Ask for the minutes to be translated into English
Assume nothing relevant to you was decided
Ask your co-teacher for a short summary afterwards
questions.why: A two-minute summary from your co-teacher is a small favor and the fastest route to the part that affects you. Assuming nothing relevant was decided is how foreign teachers find out about a schedule change from a student.

questions.stem: What most strongly predicts a foreign teacher having a good year at a Taiwanese school?
options: Turning up to things that are not lessons
Teaching experience
Chinese language ability
Having a detailed contract
questions.why: Sports day, the dinner, the rehearsal, the leaving party for someone you barely know. Each is an hour; together they are the difference between being a colleague and being a visitor. Language helps, but attendance is what people actually notice.

questions.stem: You and your co-teacher have worked together all year without ever agreeing roles. You lead every lesson; she manages behavior and rarely plans with you. It is May. Is it worth raising now?
options: No — the year is nearly over, raise it in September
Yes — but put it in writing so next year's arrangement is clear
No — the pattern is established and she clearly prefers it
Yes — ask the roles question now, framed around next year rather than as a complaint about this one
questions.why: May is arguably the best moment: there is no crisis to resolve, and next year's arrangements are being thought about anyway. Framing it forward — “for next year, could we try swapping the lead?” — makes it a plan rather than a verdict on the year you both just had. And “she prefers it” is usually a guess neither of you has ever checked.

questions.stem: Your co-teacher has become noticeably cooler over several weeks. You cannot identify anything that happened. What is the most useful response?
options: Ask directly what you did wrong
Ask a low-stakes, forward-looking question in private — and consider whether you corrected or contradicted her in front of anyone recently
Wait for it to pass; asking would make it awkward
Raise it with the Director of Academic Affairs
questions.why: Waiting rarely repairs anything and “what did I do wrong?” asks her to voice a criticism, which is exactly what the indirectness was avoiding. A private, low-stakes opening gives her a way in without cost. And the specific thing worth auditing is public correction — a moment that felt trivial to you can have been expensive for her, in front of students or colleagues.

questions.stem: It is May and nobody has mentioned your renewal. You raised it once in March and got “we'll see how things go.” What now?
options: Take it as a negative signal and start applying elsewhere
Wait; the school will tell you when it knows
Ask 人事室 directly about the timeline and paperwork, separately from asking your principal about the decision
Ask your co-teacher what she has heard
questions.why: Splitting the question is the move. The administrative timeline is a factual matter Personnel can answer plainly, and asking about it is not asking anyone to deliver news. It also frequently reveals the real state of things — a school that has begun the paperwork has effectively decided. “We'll see” about a decision is not the same signal as “we'll see” about a proposal.

questions.stem: A newly arrived foreign teacher at your school is visibly heading for trouble — skipping staff events, correcting colleagues publicly, complaining by email. What is the most useful thing you can do?
options: Leave it; it is not your business and they may resent the advice
Mention your concerns to the principal so the school can address it
Send them a link to this module
Explain the patterns privately and early, as things you got wrong yourself
questions.why: Almost every returning teacher made some of these mistakes in their own first year, and hearing it from someone who did is completely different from hearing it as a correction. Do it privately, early, and as autobiography rather than instruction. Going to the principal turns a fixable habit into a file.

questions.stem: Something in this module conflicts with what your school actually expects of you. What should you do?
options: Follow this module; it reflects the county's guidance
Follow your school — these are observed norms, not rules — and tell us about the gap
Ask the Education Department to rule on it
Follow whichever is more convenient
questions.why: This is the only module in the series with no statute behind it, and a school that does things differently is not doing them wrongly. Your school wins. But tell us — a mismatch between what we describe and what schools actually do means this page needs fixing, and the people living it are the only ones who can say so.
